case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Hawaii’s firearm licensing/carry restrictions violate the Second and Fourteenth Amendments under Bruen’s text-and-history test—and, relatedly, whether courts may rely on expert testimony that effectively supplies legal conclusions about the meaning of historical firearm regulations.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. II (right to keep and bear arms) as incorporated against the States through the Fourteenth Amendment; applied through the methodological framework announced in New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners contend that the Second Amendment’s plain text covers ordinary citizens’ possession/carry of arms for self-defense, so Hawaii’s restrictive licensing/carry regime is presumptively unconstitutional unless the State proves a well-established historical analogue. They argue Hawaii cannot meet that burden and that lower courts have been resistant to faithfully applying Heller/McDonald/Bruen by resorting to policy balancing (public-safety interests) or by accepting historical ‘expert’ testimony that crosses the Rule 702 line into impermissible legal conclusions (i.e., telling courts how to interpret founding-era statutes and whether particular historical materials satisfy Bruen).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Hawaii) defends its regulatory regime as consistent with the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation, arguing that historical restrictions support the State’s ability to condition or limit public carry/possession in the interest of public safety. Hawaii also appears to rely on a developed historical record—potentially including expert analysis—to argue that the relevant history, including later-enacted regulations where informative, demonstrates constitutionally permissible limits and that courts may consider party-built historical records and legal sources in resolving the Bruen inquiry.
key_precedents: District of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570 (2008)
McDonald v. City of Chicago, 561 U.S. 742 (2010)
New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1 (2022)
United States v. Herring, 955 F.2d 703 (11th Cir. 1992)
Commodores Entertainment Corp. v. McClary, 879 F.3d 1114 (11th Cir. 2018)
Heller v. District of Columbia (Heller II), 670 F.3d 1244 (D.C. Cir. 2011) (Kavanaugh, J., dissenting) (as quoted for original-meaning primacy)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that Bruen contemplates objective, administrable licensing as a permissible manner regulation, and that later practice may sometimes confirm an enduring tradition. But that argument turns on the factual predicate Justice Kavanaugh highlights: whether ordinary, law-abiding citizens have a realistic, non-discretionary path to obtain a permit; on this record Hawaii’s regime appears to function as a discretionary or near-prohibitory system akin to the may-issue structures Bruen rejected. The State’s proposed analogues—surety and “going armed” laws—do not burden the right in the same way or for the same reasons, as Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch emphasize: they were targeted, post hoc responses to demonstrably threatening conduct, not a broad ex ante denial by default. We can and should write narrowly (as Justice Kavanaugh urges), leaving intact background checks and other objective conditions in the abstract while holding only that a special-need or functionally unavailable public-carry scheme lacks a relevantly similar historical analogue.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that Bruen permits a context-sensitive synthesis of historical practice and that objective licensing and location limits may be justified by analogues even without a precise match. But that framing cannot relieve Hawaii of its affirmative burden to identify a well-established, representative tradition that imposed a comparably broad denial of public carry for ordinary, peaceable citizens; post-ratification drift and outlier regulations cannot substitute for the Second Amendment’s original public meaning. As Justice Gorsuch emphasizes, courts must do the legal work Bruen demands and cannot convert expert narration into a bottom-line constitutional judgment or resurrect interest balancing through ‘manner regulation’ labels. On this record, Hawaii has not shown a historically grounded analogue for a discretionary or functionally prohibitory carry regime, so the petitioners are entitled to relief.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson are right to emphasize that Bruen leaves room for objective, administrable licensing as a regulation of manner, but that point does not rescue a regime that, in design or operation, conditions carry on a showing of special need or vests open-ended discretion in officials. As the Chief Justice notes, the record here indicates Hawaii’s system functions closer to the may-issue structure Bruen condemned than to a genuine shall-issue scheme that ordinary, law-abiding citizens can actually use. And the State’s proposed analogues—surety and “going armed” laws—regulated particular threatening conduct and typically operated post hoc, not as a broad ex ante denial of the right to bear arms for self-defense. I also agree with Justice Gorsuch that historians may provide context, but courts must make the legal judgment whether the State has identified a well-established, representative historical analogue matching both the why and the how of Hawaii’s burden.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson are right to stress that Bruen leaves room for objective, administrable licensing as a manner regulation, and that later practice may sometimes illuminate a tradition; but that premise depends on a record showing a realistic path for ordinary, law-abiding citizens to obtain permits. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Hawaii’s regime appears to operate as discretionary or functionally prohibitory—closer to the may-issue systems Bruen invalidated than to a genuine shall-issue framework—and the State has not carried its burden to identify a well-established, representative analogue imposing a comparably broad ex ante denial of public carry. Surety and “going armed” laws, as Justice Gorsuch and Justice Thomas explain, were targeted, post hoc restraints keyed to threatening conduct, not default denials for peaceable citizens. Historians may supply context, but we cannot accept expert bottom lines as substitutes for the court’s analogical judgment under text, history, and tradition.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Thomas press the strongest point: surety and “going armed” laws look targeted and post hoc, so they do not justify a broad ex ante denial resembling a may-issue scheme. But that argument assumes what I do not think we can assume on this record—namely, that Hawaii’s regime is, in fact, a functional prohibition for ordinary, law-abiding citizens rather than an objective manner-of-carry licensing system of the sort Justice Kavanaugh acknowledges Bruen left room for. Bruen itself cautions against over-reading remote history and directs a context-sensitive “how and why” inquiry; that framework leaves space for Hawaii to defend objective licensing and place-based limits through representative analogues without demanding a Founding-era twin. I agree with Justice Gorsuch that judges must make the ultimate analogical judgment, yet historians can still supply the necessary contextual synthesis, and I would not strike down the scheme categorically without clearer findings on how it operates in practice.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s best point is that Bruen leaves room for objective, administrable “shall-issue” licensing and that the State need not produce a Founding-era “dead ringer.” But as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, the record here indicates Hawaii’s scheme operates as a discretionary or functionally prohibitory regime for ordinary, law-abiding citizens, which triggers Bruen’s core concern and requires the State to produce a representative historical tradition imposing a comparably broad ex ante denial for comparable reasons. The State’s principal analogues—surety and “going armed” laws—were targeted and typically post hoc responses to demonstrably threatening conduct, not blanket gatekeeping that withholds the right by default. And while I agree with Justice Kagan that historians can provide context, we cannot outsource the step-two analogical judgment or dilute the State’s burden through expert bottom-line assertions.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson make the best point that Bruen contemplates objective, administrable shall-issue licensing and that history can be assessed context-sensitively rather than by demanding a Founding-era “twin.” But that framing still turns the case on whether Hawaii’s scheme, as designed and administered, provides ordinary, law-abiding citizens a realistic path to carry for self-defense; if it retains special-need features or operates through open-ended discretion, it falls on the may-issue side Bruen rejected, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize. The surety and “going armed” laws do not supply a relevantly similar analogue because they were targeted, post hoc tools aimed at demonstrably threatening conduct, not a broad ex ante denial by default. I also agree with Justice Jackson’s evidentiary point: historians can inform the record, but the ultimate “relevantly similar” analogue judgment is a legal determination for courts, not an expert’s bottom line.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson are right that Bruen allows analogical reasoning and that objective, administrable licensing may be consistent with the Second Amendment if it truly regulates manner rather than operates as a default denial. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, the constitutional hinge here is functional availability: on this record Hawaii’s regime appears to operate like a may-issue or near-prohibitory system for ordinary, law-abiding citizens, and the State therefore bears (and has not carried) the burden to show a representative tradition imposing a comparably broad ex ante restraint. The asserted historical analogues—surety and going-armed laws aimed at demonstrably threatening conduct, plus late/outlier measures—do not match in “why” or “how” a regime that effectively conditions carry on special need. I also agree with Justice Gorsuch that historians can supply context, but their bottom-line assertions cannot substitute for the court’s own Bruen step-two constitutional judgment.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The most forceful point from the Petitioners—pressed by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas—is that Hawaii’s system allegedly operates as a functional ban for ordinary, law-abiding citizens, and that surety or “going armed” laws cannot serve as relevantly similar analogues for an ex ante, broad denial. I take that seriously, but I remain unpersuaded that Bruen compels invalidation on this record without a clearer, administrable showing that Hawaii’s regime is in fact discretionary or practically unavailable in the way Bruen condemned, rather than a potentially objective licensing framework that regulates the manner of carry. At step two, I do not read Bruen to demand a Founding-era “twin”; the State may satisfy its burden with well-established, representative traditions of regulating public carry to prevent terrorizing or dangerous public carry, so long as the “why” and “how” are analogous and the regime is not a pretext for denial. I agree with Justice Kavanaugh that the constitutional fault line is discretionary, special-need licensing versus objective, shall-issue administration, and I would not constitutionalize a presumption of functional prohibition absent a developed factual predicate.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Second Amendment’s plain text covers ordinary law-abiding citizens’ carrying handguns in public for self-defense, so Hawaii must justify its licensing/carry restrictions by showing they are consistent with the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation under Bruen. To the extent Hawaii’s regime operates as a discretionary or functionally prohibitory system that denies typical applicants absent a special need, it resembles the “may-issue” regimes Bruen held unconstitutional and is not rescued by the surety or “going armed” analogues, which were targeted, post hoc, and aimed at demonstrably threatening conduct rather than broadly burdening the public generally. Hawaii may of course build a historical record, but courts must independently perform the legal, analogical reasoning Bruen requires; expert testimony cannot supply legal conclusions about what the Second Amendment means or whether a given historical practice is a sufficient analogue. Because Hawaii has not carried its burden to identify a relevantly similar historical analogue—matching both the why and how of the restriction—the challenged scheme violates the Second and Fourteenth Amendments.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Second Amendment’s text protects ordinary, law-abiding citizens’ right to “keep and bear Arms,” and carrying a handgun in public for self-defense falls within that plain meaning. Under Bruen’s text-and-history test, Hawaii must justify its restrictive licensing/carry regime by identifying a well-established historical analogue from the Founding era (and, as relevant to incorporation, 1868) that similarly denies ordinary citizens the ability to carry absent discretionary or onerous conditions; generalized appeals to public safety and interest balancing are constitutionally irrelevant. The historical record does not support a broad tradition of near-prohibitory public-carry licensing for ordinary citizens, and Hawaii cannot evade the constitutional inquiry by offering later-enacted or outlier regulations as substitutes for the relevant original public meaning. Courts also may not outsource Bruen’s legal judgment to “experts” who opine on what the Constitution permits or whether a regulation satisfies Bruen, because that is a legal conclusion for judges applying text and history, not a factual question resolved by expert say-so.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Second Amendment’s text covers ordinary, law-abiding citizens’ right to “bear” arms for self-defense, including in public, so Hawaii’s carry-licensing restrictions are presumptively unconstitutional unless the State can justify them by a well-established historical analogue under Bruen. To the extent Hawaii’s regime functionally denies most citizens the ability to carry absent a showing of “special need” beyond ordinary self-defense or otherwise vests licensing officials with open-ended discretion, it mirrors the very “may-issue” structure Bruen held unconstitutional and cannot be saved by modern public-safety balancing. Hawaii may introduce historical materials, and experts may help identify and contextualize sources, but courts must independently decide the legal meaning of those sources and cannot treat expert “opinions” that Heller/McDonald/Bruen were wrong—or that particular historical laws satisfy Bruen—as dispositive legal conclusions. Because Hawaii has not shown a relevantly similar historical tradition supporting a discretionary or special-need carry regime for ordinary citizens, the challenged restrictions violate the Second and Fourteenth Amendments.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under Bruen’s text-and-history framework, the Second Amendment’s plain text presumptively covers ordinary law-abiding citizens’ carrying of handguns for self-defense in public, shifting the burden to Hawaii to show its licensing/carry restrictions are consistent with this Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation. On the present record, Hawaii’s regime—particularly if it operates in practice to deny most typical applicants the ability to carry—resembles the kind of “may-issue” system Bruen found unconstitutional because it broadly divests the right rather than imposing a historically grounded, objective regulation. Hawaii may rely on historians to supply historical facts and context, but courts must themselves perform the legal analogical reasoning Bruen requires; expert testimony that effectively dictates whether history “satisfies Bruen” risks substituting an expert’s legal conclusion for the judiciary’s duty. Because Hawaii has not carried its burden to identify a genuinely analogous historical tradition supporting a near-general denial of public carry for ordinary citizens, the challenged restrictions violate the Second and Fourteenth Amendments.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under Bruen, once Hawaii shows that its licensing/carry limits regulate the manner of public carry rather than amount to a flat prohibition for ordinary, law-abiding citizens, the State may justify the regime by identifying historical analogues using Bruen’s “how and why” inquiry—without collapsing the analysis into free-form interest balancing. In conducting that inquiry, courts should not treat a single historical “snapshot” (whether 1791 or 1868) as mechanically dispositive; Bruen itself cautions that evidence long predating the relevant ratification period may be unilluminating, while later practice may sometimes help confirm the tradition, so the proper approach is a context-sensitive synthesis of the most relevant periods rather than wheel-spinning over remote outliers. On the evidentiary question, expert historians may assist courts by supplying context, translations, and factual synthesis about historical sources, but Rule 702 does not permit experts to dictate the legal meaning of the Second or Fourteenth Amendments or to pronounce that a given set of statutes “satisfies Bruen”—those are legal conclusions for judges. Applying that framework here, Hawaii may rely on a developed historical record (including expert assistance on facts) to support analogues for regulating public carry through objective licensing and sensitive-place/location restrictions, so I would not invalidate the regime on the premise that all such regulations are categorically foreclosed or that expert-assisted history is per se improper.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Second Amendment’s text covers ordinary, law-abiding citizens’ carrying of arms for self-defense, so Hawaii’s restrictive licensing/carry regime is presumptively unconstitutional unless the State can show it accords with the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation under Bruen. On this record—where Hawaii has represented that it has already put forward all the evidence it has—the State has not identified historical analogues imposing a comparable burden and comparably justified limits (as opposed to broad public-disarmament by default), and courts may not “game away” the right by reverting to interest balancing under the guise of public safety. Nor may courts outsource the legal meaning of founding-era statutes to experts: historical experts can help identify sources and context, but Rule 702 does not permit testimony that supplies legal conclusions about what historical laws mean or whether they satisfy Bruen’s constitutional standard, a duty that belongs to judges. Given the posture and the State’s failure to carry its burden under Bruen’s text-and-history inquiry, petitioners are entitled to relief at least as to applications disarming ordinary citizens who seek to carry for lawful self-defense.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Heller and McDonald, the Second Amendment protects an individual right to possess and carry firearms for self-defense, and Bruen requires Hawaii to justify any public-carry licensing restrictions by pointing to a well-established historical analogue that is “relevantly similar” in burden and justification. To the extent Hawaii’s regime (including any post-Bruen revisions) either retains discretionary “special need” features or operates in practice with open-ended official discretion that makes permits effectively unavailable to ordinary, law-abiding citizens, it is constitutionally problematic; objective “shall-issue” features such as fingerprinting, background checks, and training generally remain permissible, but not a functional re-creation of a may-issue system. Hawaii has not carried its burden if it relies primarily on generalized public-safety balancing or late-arising regulatory trends untethered to the Founding-era understanding of the right to bear arms. And while courts may consider historical experts for authentication and context, Bruen’s legal conclusion about what the history means is for judges to decide—expert testimony cannot substitute for the required judicial determination of historical tradition.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Second Amendment’s text covers ordinary, law-abiding citizens’ public carry of commonly used arms for self-defense, so Hawaii’s restrictive licensing/carry regime is presumptively unconstitutional and the State bears the affirmative burden to justify it by showing consistency with the Amendment’s historical understanding. On the record described, Hawaii has not met that burden because the principal asserted “analogues” (a Reconstruction-era Black Code and a narrow anti-poaching/trespass measure) are late, outlier, or constitutionally disqualified sources that do not reflect a representative tradition of broadly disarming peaceable citizens in ordinary public places. Bruen allows principle-based analogical reasoning, but it does not permit converting isolated, discriminatory, or materially different regulations into a general tradition supporting a default ban on carry. Courts may consider expert historical testimony to authenticate sources and provide context, but they may not defer to experts for the legal conclusion whether the history satisfies Bruen’s standard; that is a judicial determination, and reliance on expert “bottom-line” legal characterizations cannot substitute for the State’s burden of producing historically grounded analogues.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Applying Bruen’s controlling framework, ordinary citizens’ public carry for self-defense is conduct presumptively covered by the Second Amendment’s plain text, so Hawaii bears the burden to justify its licensing/carry restrictions by showing consistency with the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation through well-established, representative analogues rather than a precise historical match. On the present record as described, Hawaii plausibly can satisfy that burden insofar as its regime operates as an objective, administrable licensing system and is supported by historically recognized limits on public carry (and related public-safety regulations), which Bruen itself indicated could be constitutionally permissible if not administered as open-ended discretion. Separately, courts may consider expert historical testimony to assemble and explain historical sources, but they must police Rule 702 boundaries: experts cannot supply the legal conclusion about what the Second Amendment means or whether the State has met Bruen’s analogue requirement—those are judicial determinations that must be made in a clear, workable way for lower courts and legislatures. Because Hawaii’s approach can be evaluated under Bruen via representative analogues without turning constitutional meaning over to experts, I would uphold the regime as applied here.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Hawaii’s restrictions on the public carrying of firearms violate the Second Amendment under the history-and-tradition test announced in Bruen, and whether courts may rely on expert testimony that effectively supplies legal conclusions about historical meaning.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. II (as incorporated against the States through the Fourteenth Amendment); Federal Rule of Evidence 702 (as to the admissibility/scope of expert testimony in Second Amendment historical analysis).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that Hawaii’s carry restrictions burden conduct covered by the Second Amendment’s plain text (bearing arms for self-defense) and therefore are presumptively unconstitutional unless Hawaii proves a well-established historical tradition of analogous regulation. They contend Hawaii cannot meet Bruen’s historical burden and that lower courts err when they dilute Heller/McDonald/Bruen with interest-balancing or generalized public-safety rationales. Petitioners (and supporting amici) also argue that much of Hawaii’s proffered expert evidence impermissibly crosses from historical fact into legal argument—telling courts how to interpret founding-era laws—so it should be excluded under Rule 702 because statutory and constitutional interpretation is the court’s job, not an expert’s.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Hawaii) is positioned to argue that its public-carry regulatory scheme fits within the Second Amendment as historically understood because there is a tradition of regulating the manner, places, and conditions of public carry (especially to protect public safety), and that the law is consistent with analogous historical restrictions. Hawaii also appears to defend the use of historians or other experts to develop the historical record and support the claim that the challenged regulations align with historical practices, contending that such testimony assists the court in understanding complex historical sources even if ultimate constitutional interpretation remains for judges.
key_precedents: District of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570 (2008)
McDonald v. City of Chicago, 561 U.S. 742 (2010)
New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass'n, Inc. v. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1 (2022)
Commodores Entertainment Corp. v. McClary, 879 F.3d 1114 (11th Cir. 2018)
United States v. Herring, 955 F.2d 703 (11th Cir. 1992)
Heller v. District of Columbia (Heller II), 670 F.3d 1224 (D.C. Cir. 2011) (Kavanaugh, J., dissenting)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito press the strongest point: Bruen does not permit converting historically targeted surety/going-armed measures and discrete sensitive-place rules into a de facto statewide ban on ordinary public carry, and generalized safety rationales cannot substitute for historical tradition. But that objection turns on an operational characterization—whether Hawaii’s regime actually functions as a practical nullity for law-abiding citizens—which, as Justice Kagan notes, is statute- and record-dependent and not clearly established here in a way that warrants facial invalidation. Under Rahimi’s warning against demanding a historical “dead ringer,” a licensing-plus-location/manner framework can be relevantly similar in why and how to traditions aimed at preventing public terror and addressing demonstrated threats, so long as courts rigorously police overbreadth and prevent “sensitive places” from swallowing the right. I would affirm with clear limiting guidance and strict Rule 702 gatekeeping (as Kagan and Kavanaugh also note) to ensure historians supply facts and context, not the ultimate analogue judgment.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s strongest point is his characterization of Hawaii’s scheme as an objective licensing-plus-location framework that could, under Rahimi, be supported without a historical “dead ringer.” But Bruen still places the burden on the State to show a relevantly similar tradition in both how and why the law burdens the right, and—consistent with Justice Alito and Justice Gorsuch’s observations—the principal analogues (surety/going-armed laws and discrete sensitive-place restrictions) were typically conditional and targeted to particularized threats or terrorizing conduct, not a default criminal prohibition across most ordinary destinations. If “sensitive places” expand so broadly that ordinary public carry becomes practically illusory, that is a material mismatch in mechanism and severity that generalized public-safety rationales cannot cure. I also agree with the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan that historians may assist with facts and context, but Rule 702 cannot be used to outsource the ultimate analogue judgment or constitutional meaning, which remains ours—and on this record the State has not carried its historical burden.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s strongest point is that Hawaii’s scheme can be characterized as objective licensing plus targeted location and manner limits, with surety and going-armed laws supplying relevant analogues, and Rahimi cautions against demanding a historical “dead ringer.” But as Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, those historical measures were conditional—typically triggered by individualized suspicion or terrorizing conduct—and they did not impose a default criminal prohibition on ordinary public carry by law-abiding citizens across the ordinary places they must travel and live. Even accepting the Chief’s record-framing concern, Bruen places the burden on the State to show a tradition relevantly similar in both “how” and “why,” and the State has not shown a tradition supporting a regime that risks making public carry practically illusory through expansive “sensitive place” designations. I agree with Justice Kagan that historians may assist with historical facts and context, but that evidentiary point cannot cure the State’s failure to identify a comparably burdensome, historically grounded analogue.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito press the case’s hardest point: surety and going-armed/Northampton-style laws were generally conditional and targeted, and a State cannot relabel a near-total public-carry ban as mere “place-and-manner” regulation or let “sensitive places” swallow the right. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Bruen (as clarified by Rahimi) demands an analogical inquiry attentive to “how” and “why,” not a one-to-one historical twin, and this record permits viewing Hawaii’s regime as licensing plus genuinely discrete location limits rather than a categorical divestment of ordinary citizens’ right to bear arms. The proper disposition, in my view, is to affirm while making explicit that lower courts must test operationally whether the scheme leaves a meaningful avenue for public carry and must invalidate overbroad sensitive-place designations that function as a de facto ban. I also agree with Roberts/Kagan that Rule 702 allows historians to supply facts and context, but not ultimate constitutional meaning or the analogue judgment, which remains ours.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The strongest point from Justice Thomas and Justice Alito is that Bruen will not tolerate recasting a near-prohibition as “place-and-manner,” and that surety/going-armed laws were typically conditional—triggered by particularized suspicion or terrorizing conduct—rather than default bans on ordinary carry. But as the Chief Justice emphasizes, that critique depends on an operational characterization not clearly resolved on this record: whether Hawaii’s licensing-plus-location scheme leaves ordinary, law-abiding citizens a meaningful avenue to bear arms and whether the claimed analogues match in both how and why they burden the right. I would affirm in substantial part while expressly instructing lower courts that “sensitive places” cannot swallow the rule and that any scheme functioning as a de facto ban fails under Bruen, notwithstanding generalized public-safety rationales. I also align with Roberts/Kavanaugh/Barrett that Rule 702 may permit historians to supply facts and context, but courts must prevent experts from opining on ultimate constitutional meaning or dictating the analogue judgment.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s strongest point is that Hawaii’s scheme can be characterized as a historically familiar place-and-manner framework, and Rahimi cautions us not to demand a “dead ringer.” But even accepting that framing, Bruen still assigns the State the burden to identify a tradition imposing a comparably justified and comparably burdensome restraint, and—as Justice Thomas and Justice Alito emphasize—the principal candidates (surety and going-armed laws) were typically conditioned on individualized suspicion or terrorizing conduct, not a default criminal prohibition across broad swaths of ordinary life. If Hawaii’s sensitive-place designations and default prohibitions operate as petitioners allege—making public carry largely illusory—the mismatch in both “how” and “why” is dispositive under Bruen, and generalized public-safety rationales cannot fill the historical gap. I agree with Justice Kagan and the Chief that historians may assist with facts and context under Rule 702, but they cannot supply the ultimate analogue judgment or constitutional meaning, which remains ours.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s argument (echoed by Justice Kagan) that Hawaii’s scheme should be operationally characterized as objective licensing plus targeted place-and-manner limits is the State’s strongest point, and Rahimi correctly warns against demanding a historical “dead ringer.” But even on that framing, Bruen requires the State to carry its burden by showing relevant similarity in both why and how: the surety and going-armed laws generally turned on individualized suspicion or terrorizing conduct and did not impose a default criminal prohibition across the ordinary places law-abiding citizens live and travel. If the “sensitive places” designations and default prohibitions function to make ordinary public carry largely illusory, that is a materially heavier burden than the historical analogues and the State’s historical showing remains insufficient. I agree with the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan on Rule 702: historians may supply historical facts and context, but not the ultimate analogue judgment or constitutional meaning, which is for courts.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s strongest point is that, under Rahimi, Hawaii need not identify a historical “dead ringer,” and that an objective licensing-plus-location scheme could be analogized to surety/going-armed laws and genuine sensitive-place restrictions. But as Justice Thomas and Justice Alito emphasize, those historical measures were typically conditional—triggered by particularized threats or terrorizing conduct—and their “how” (mechanism and burden) does not match a default criminal prohibition that sweeps across most ordinary public destinations. On this record, the State has not affirmatively carried Bruen’s burden to show a founding-era tradition supporting a comparably heavy, across-the-board restriction while leaving a meaningful avenue to “bear” arms for self-defense. I agree with Justice Kagan (and the Chief) that historians may assist on facts and context, but Rule 702 cannot supply the ultimate analogue judgment; given the State’s thin showing, I would not uphold the regime based on characterization disputes better resolved with a developed evidentiary record.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s strongest point is that surety/going-armed/Northampton-type laws were typically conditional and targeted, so they cannot be bootstrapped into a regime that effectively criminalizes ordinary public carry everywhere an ordinary person needs to go. I accept that premise—and I share the concern that “sensitive places” cannot be defined so broadly that they swallow the right—but, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, that is an operational, record-dependent characterization question, and this record does not yet establish the kind of practical foreclosure that would justify facial invalidation at this stage. Consistent with Rahimi’s warning against requiring a historical “dead ringer,” I would affirm while making explicit that lower courts must police overbreadth and require the State to show a meaningful avenue to carry for self-defense; if the scheme functions as a de facto ban, it fails under Bruen. On the evidentiary issue, I align with Roberts/Kagan that Rule 702 demands strict gatekeeping—historians can supply facts and context, but not ultimate constitutional meaning—yet that problem is best addressed through cabining testimony rather than striking the law absent a developed showing of practical nullification.

John Roberts.reasoning: Because Hawaii’s restrictions regulate conduct covered by the Second Amendment’s plain text (bearing arms in public for self-defense), the State bears the burden under Bruen to identify a historical tradition that is “relevantly similar” in why and how it burdens that right. On this record, a licensing-and-location regime that targets the manner and places of public carry—rather than imposing a near-total public carry ban—fits within the longstanding tradition of regulating public carry to mitigate demonstrated threats of physical violence, including surety and going-armed laws and historically recognized limits on carrying in particular sensitive settings; the Second Amendment right was never understood to sweep indiscriminately. As to experts, courts may receive historians’ assistance on historical facts (what laws existed, how they were applied, what terms meant), but Rule 702 does not permit experts to supply the ultimate legal meaning of the Second Amendment or to instruct courts how to interpret founding-era law—those conclusions remain for judges applying Bruen’s analogical test. Applying those principles, Hawaii’s use of expert testimony is permissible only to the extent it informs the historical record, while the carry restrictions themselves are consistent with historical tradition as a targeted regulation rather than a broad prohibition.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Hawaii’s regime restricts the ordinary, law-abiding citizen’s ability to carry firearms in public for self-defense, conduct the Second Amendment’s plain text protects as “bear[ing] Arms,” so the restriction is presumptively unconstitutional under Bruen. Hawaii therefore bears the burden to identify a well-established American historical tradition of genuinely comparable regulation, measured by both how and why the asserted analogues burdened the right; broad public-carry prohibitions cannot be justified by materially different measures like surety or bond statutes that merely conditioned carry for those credibly suspected of threatening harm. Nor may courts dilute Bruen’s inquiry with generalized public-safety rationales or allow expert testimony to supply the ultimate legal meaning of historical sources, because interpreting statutes and the Constitution is the court’s responsibility rather than an expert’s under Rule 702. On this record and in light of Bruen’s rejection of surety and Northampton-style analogues as support for sweeping carry restrictions, Hawaii has not carried its historical burden.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under Bruen, petitioners’ proposed conduct—carrying handguns in public for self-defense—falls within the Second Amendment’s plain text, so Hawaii bears the burden to identify a well-established historical tradition of analogous restrictions. Hawaii’s post-Bruen scheme, described as making carry licenses effectively useless by broadly criminalizing carry in most public places, resembles the sort of functional public-disarmament regime that Bruen rejected and is not justified by a general appeal to public safety or by stretching “sensitive places” beyond historically grounded limits. To the extent lower courts relied on expert testimony that supplies legal conclusions about what the Second Amendment or founding-era enactments “mean,” that use conflicts with the judge’s duty to interpret the law; experts may assist with historical facts and sources, but Rule 702 does not permit experts to dictate the constitutional standard or its application. Because Hawaii has not shown a historical analogue sufficient to sustain so sweeping a burden on the core right of armed self-defense, the restrictions violate the Second Amendment.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Applying Bruen’s text-and-history framework, Hawaii may regulate public carry if it can show a historical tradition of analogous limits on the manner, locations, and conditions of carrying arms, and Rahimi confirms that the analogue inquiry is not a demand for a one-to-one historical twin. On this record, the challenged scheme appears aimed at channeling where and how firearms may be carried in public rather than broadly divesting ordinary, law-abiding citizens of the right to bear arms altogether—an important distinction in assessing the Amendment’s historical scope. As to expert testimony, Rule 702 permits historians to assist courts in understanding sources and context, but courts must not outsource the ultimate constitutional meaning to experts; properly cabined, such testimony can develop the historical record without supplying binding legal conclusions. Because Hawaii’s approach plausibly fits within historically recognized limitations and the evidentiary concerns can be managed by policing the line between historical fact and legal interpretation, I would vote to uphold Hawaii’s position here.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Bruen supplies the controlling standard: once the conduct (public carry) is covered by the Second Amendment’s plain text, the State must justify its regulation by showing a historical tradition of relevantly analogous restrictions, with special attention to how governments historically regulated the manner and locations of carrying weapons to protect public safety. On this record, Hawaii’s regime can be sustained to the extent it operates as a place-and-manner system with recognizable historical analogues (e.g., longstanding restrictions on carrying in sensitive places and regulations aimed at preventing public terror), rather than a discretionary “may-issue” denial of ordinary citizens’ ability to carry at all. And Rule 702 does not categorically bar historians: courts may receive expert testimony to help decode unfamiliar sources and practices, but must police it to ensure the expert does not supply the ultimate legal meaning of the Second Amendment or dictate which analogues are constitutionally dispositive—those are judicial judgments under Bruen’s test. Because the challenge as framed seeks to exclude such assistance wholesale and to invalidate Hawaii’s restrictions without the historically grounded, statute-specific analogue analysis Bruen requires, I would vote to affirm in substantial part and clarify the proper limits on expert testimony.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Hawaii’s restrictions regulate ordinary public carry for self-defense—conduct the Second Amendment’s text covers as “bearing” arms—so under Bruen the State bears the burden to justify its regime by demonstrating a historical tradition of analogous regulation. On this record, Hawaii’s effort to convert shall-issue licensing into a near-general ban by declaring broad swaths of public space off-limits appears to impose a materially heavier burden than the historically accepted surety/“going armed” and other manner-based regulations, and the State’s asserted public-safety rationale cannot substitute for the required showing of a comparably justified, comparably burdensome historical analogue. Because the State leans heavily on expert declarations that stray from assisting with historical facts into supplying legal conclusions about constitutional meaning, courts should treat such testimony with caution under Rule 702—the interpretation of text and historical sources is ultimately the judiciary’s task. Applying these principles, Hawaii has not carried its Bruen burden to show the challenged restrictions are consistent with this Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation, and the restrictions therefore violate the Second Amendment at least in substantial applications central to the right.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Second Amendment’s plain text covers ordinary, law-abiding citizens’ conduct of bearing arms in public for self-defense, so Hawaii must justify its carry restrictions by identifying a well-established historical tradition of “relevantly similar” regulation, not by invoking public-safety balancing. Under Bruen, broad regimes that effectively deny typical citizens the ability to carry (or that impose discretionary, open-ended permitting) lack sufficient founding-era or Reconstruction-era analogues; historical examples like surety and going-armed laws were narrow, targeted, and did not operate as a general prohibition on public carry. Hawaii may regulate through objective, non-discretionary “shall-issue” licensing and through historically recognized categories such as sensitive places, but it cannot convert those categories into a near-ban on public carry. As to expert testimony, courts may use historians to explain sources and context, but Rule 702 does not permit experts to supply legal conclusions about constitutional meaning—the interpretive judgment under Bruen is for judges applying text, history, and precedent.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Hawaii’s public-carry restrictions regulate conduct presumptively protected by the Second Amendment’s plain text—“bearing” arms for ordinary self-defense in public—so, under Bruen, Hawaii bears the burden to affirmatively prove its regime is consistent with the Nation’s founding-era historical tradition of firearm regulation. On this record as described, Hawaii’s justification appears to rely heavily on generalized public-safety rationales and later-in-time regulatory practice rather than well-established founding-era analogues that imposed a comparably broad constraint on ordinary, law-abiding citizens’ public carry; without a persuasive founding-era pedigree (or an independently justified use of later history to liquidate an ambiguity), the State has not carried its burden. Nor may courts outsource the constitutional meaning of historical materials to experts: historians may assist with factual context and source authentication, but Rule 702 does not permit expert testimony to supply legal conclusions about what the Second Amendment “means” or whether an analogue is sufficiently similar—those are judicial determinations under Bruen’s framework. Because Hawaii has not affirmatively shown its restrictions fit within the pre-existing limits that defined the right at ratification, I would vote to hold the restrictions unconstitutional (or at minimum require proper application of Bruen with permissible evidentiary boundaries).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Applying Bruen as controlling law while remaining attentive to practical consequences and procedural fairness, I would uphold Hawaii’s public-carry restrictions if—on this record—they operate as objective, evenhanded conditions on carrying in public rather than a discretionary scheme that denies ordinary, law-abiding residents any meaningful avenue to carry for self-defense. The history-and-tradition inquiry must be conducted with methodological rigor, but it should also recognize the longstanding tradition of regulating the manner and sensitive locations of public carry to protect public safety in densely populated settings, which Hawaii plausibly invokes as an analogue. On expert testimony, Rule 702 permits historians to help courts understand sources, context, and empirical historical facts, but courts must exclude or cabin opinions that cross the line into telling judges what the Second Amendment “means” as a matter of law—because that legal judgment is the court’s responsibility and admitting such testimony risks substituting credentialed advocacy for adjudication. Given those constraints, I would not categorically bar historical experts, but I would require careful gatekeeping and would not strike down Hawaii’s regime absent a showing that it functionally forecloses the right to bear arms for self-defense for ordinary citizens.
